spec.name: Madreperla Piano Accordion
spec.description: A full-size 41-key, 120-bass piano accordion in Italian mother-of-pearl style: iridescent pearl-mosaic cases trimmed in gold and chrome, gold fan grilles, and a ruby-red gold-edged bellows, shown on the floor with its straps.
spec.layout: STATIC OBJECT, no joints. It stands on y=0 on its two case bottoms, bellows axis along X, in a symmetric composition. The front (+Z) is the grille side, shown to the audience. The treble (right-hand) case sits at -X with the 41-key piano keyboard on its -X end face. The bass (left-hand) case sits at +X with the 120 bass buttons on its +X end face. The bellows spans x -0.14..+0.14 between them, a little open. The back (-Z) carries straps and hardware, which stand 0.05 m out. Heights: treble case 0.54, bass case 0.50, bellows 0.02..0.49, so the silhouette steps down from treble to bass. Cases are 0.30 deep (z -0.15..0.15), 0.21 wide each. The Italian mother-of-pearl style shows in four ways. (1) Every case surface (top, bottom, back, front bezel, end-plate margins) is a pearl MOSAIC: a base slab in pearlShadow, covered with small raised tiles about 0.035 x 0.03 m and 2 mm thick, with 1-2 mm gaps showing the base. Tile colours are chosen deterministically by rng: 50% pearlWhite, 20% pearlCream, 10% each of pearlPink, pearlAqua and pearlLilac. Both cases use this same rule so they read as one set. (2) Every case edge has gold piping (thin 6 mm rods in goldBright) with goldDeep shadow rods beside it. Rhinestones (rhinestoneBlue and rhinestoneRose) sit as small faceted gems at the case corners and the grille centres. (3) The grilles are gold slats on a dark grilleBack recess, with a rosette in the middle. (4) The bellows is ruby red with gold-leaf edging and gold-and-pearl corner guards. Chrome is used for switches, buckles and hooks. Keep every shape simple and blocky: boxes, wedges, short cylinders of 6-10 sides. All the character comes from small coloured parts seated on the faces.

parts.builds: The right-hand (treble) case, a blocky box x -0.35..-0.14, y 0..0.54, z -0.15..0.15. It is pearl-mosaic covered on top, bottom, back and the -X end margins (the keyboard part sits on the -X face at x=-0.35, so leave the keyboard window x -0.35, y 0.03..0.51, z -0.115..0.115 free; mosaic tiles surround it). The bellows-side face at x=-0.14 is a plain pearlCream frame lip 0.012 m deep, which the bellows end frame meets. FRONT +Z: an inset pearl bezel and a dark grilleBack recess about 0.17 wide x 0.44 tall. In the recess sit about 13 goldBright slats radiating as a fan from a point near the bottom centre, each a thin 6-sided rod or box, with a goldDeep shadow slat under alternating ones. A rosette in the middle is a stack of goldBright and goldDeep 10-sided discs with a rhinestoneBlue centre. A labelCream nameplate reading 'BELLINI' (a small gold-bordered plate with tiny black bar glyphs for letters) sits below it on the bezel. TOP (+Y): a chrome register-switch bank at trebleTopSwitches, a 0.12 x 0.05 chrome plate with 6 pearlWhite rocker tabs, each with a tiny goldBright dot, and one larger master switch. Gold piping on every case edge and a rhinestone at each of the 4 top corners and 4 bottom corners, alternating rhinestoneBlue and rhinestoneRose. Four small black rubber feet (0.012 high) are sunk into the bottom so the case rests on y=0. BACK -Z: a goldDeep serial plate and two chrome strap hooks' base plates at shoulderStrapTopA/B and shoulderStrapBottomA/B (the harness part builds the straps themselves). Keep mosaic tiles merged by colour to save parts.
parts.attaches: The keyboard part sits on the -X face (mount keyboardPlane). The bellows meets the +X face at trebleBellowsFace. The harness hooks at the shoulderStrapTop/Bottom mounts on the back face.

parts.builds: The 41-key piano keyboard on the treble case's -X end face. It is a mother-of-pearl-framed keybed: 24 white keys (keyWhite) and 17 black keys (keyBlack). Keys are 0.02 pitch along Y, starting at y=0.03 (the lowest key) up to y=0.51. White keys are boxes about 0.0185 tall (y) x 0.20 long (z -0.10..0.10) x 0.03 thick (x -0.385..-0.355), with 1.5 mm gaps between them showing the felt keybed. Black keys follow the standard grouping (2 black, gap, 3 black, gap, repeating, starting after the first white key as an F-sharp pattern). Each is 0.011 tall (y), 0.11 long (z, sitting on the +Z half: z -0.01..0.10), and 0.045 thick (x -0.40..-0.355). Each black key has a thin chromeDark highlight strip on its top face and its tip is slightly bevelled with a wedge. The keybed is a felt slab (x -0.355..-0.35, y 0.03..0.51, z -0.115..0.115). Framing it: a goldBright rail along the top and bottom ends (y 0.51..0.52 and 0.02..0.03), a pearl-mosaic cap rail along the back z -0.115..-0.125 and along the front z 0.115..0.125 (pearlCream tiles with gold piping, using the same mosaic rule as the cases), and tiny rhinestones at the 4 corners of the frame. A thin labelCream key-cover felt strip with a goldDeep line sits between the keys and the +Z rail. Optionally include small goldBright pitch-marker dots on every C white key's end.
parts.attaches: Sits flush on the treble case -X face at keyboardPlane; its back x=-0.35 touches the case. The top and bottom rails stay inside the case's y range.

parts.builds: The ruby-red folding bellows between the cases, x -0.14..0.14, y 0.02..0.49, z -0.125..0.125, with corner guards reaching 0.13. It is slightly open, with 13 pleats. Each pleat is a sharp V crest, ridge at the full outline (z +-0.125, y 0.02..0.49), valley inset 0.02 m on all four sides. Build each as 4 thin tapered slabs per side or as rectangular loft rings alternating bellowsRed (outer faces), bellowsRedLight (top-facing facets) and bellowsRedDark (valley faces), so every crest reads as a ridge. Along each crest edge a thin goldBright wire (4 mm rod) runs round all four sides, and gold leaf dots sit in every other valley on the front. The four long corners of the bellows each carry corner guards, one every 0.04 m along X: small pearlCream-and-goldBright L-shaped brackets (a box 0.012 x 0.02 and a gold rivet) over the crests, so the corner reads as a gold-and-pearl bound edge. Each end has a pearlCream end frame, a rectangular ring 0.01 deep at x=-0.14 and x=+0.14, with goldBright piping and a thin black felt gasket line. Black reinforcing tape lines run along the top of the bellows on the valley folds. On the front +Z face of the bellows, a centred gold diamond lozenge motif made of 3 small gold diamond extrudes sits at x=0 on the centre pleat, flanked by 2 rhinestoneRose gems.
parts.attaches: End frames meet the treble case at trebleBellowsFace (x=-0.14) and the bass case at bassBellowsFace (x=0.14). The harness bellows strap lies across its top near x=-0.06..0.2.

parts.builds: The left-hand (bass) case, a blocky box x 0.14..0.35, y 0..0.50, z -0.15..0.15, built in the same pearl-mosaic rule and gold piping as the treble case (tile ~0.035, 2 mm raised, same colour split) on top, bottom, back and front bezel. The bellows-side face at x=0.14 is a plain pearlCream lip 0.012 deep. FRONT +Z: an inset pearl bezel and grilleBack recess 0.17 x 0.40, filled with about 9 horizontal-ish goldBright slats (a ladder pattern, slightly fanned) and a smaller rosette with a rhinestoneRose centre. END FACE +X (x=0.35, bassButtonPlane): a pearl-mosaic margin framing a dark felt recess plate, 0.25 (z) x 0.46 (y). It carries 120 bass buttons in 6 rows (z -0.09..+0.09, 0.036 pitch) of 20 (y 0.03..0.47, 0.022 pitch). Each is an 8-sided cylinder, radius 0.0085, height 0.012, projecting to x~0.362 (the part's box reaches 0.38 to allow a little button travel clearance): pearlWhite for most, chrome for the C buttons (every 3rd column in rows 3-4) and goldBright for the E buttons in rows 5-6; each button has a thin chromeDark ring base disc. All buttons of one colour are merged into one part. An air-release button sits at the top rear of the end plate (y 0.478, z -0.10): a red bellowsRedLight disc in a goldBright ring. The case has a top gold piping, rhinestones at its 8 corners (rhinestoneBlue and rhinestoneRose alternating), four black rubber feet sunk into the bottom so the case rests on y=0, and a small goldDeep brand plate on the back. On the back face, a pearl-mosaic region leaves the strap pad area at bassStrapPad free for the harness.
parts.attaches: Bellows end frame meets the -X face at bassBellowsFace (x=0.14). The harness hand-strap pad and bellows strap anchor are on its back and top at bassStrapPad and bellowsStrapAnchor. Buttons rise from the plate at bassButtonPlane (x=0.35).

parts.builds: All the straps and the hardware on them, kept to the back (-Z, out to z=-0.20) and the bellows top. (a) Two shoulder straps, each 0.045 wide and 0.008 thick strapBlack, with stitched goldDeep edge lines and a thin chromeDark centre line. Each runs from its top hook (shoulderStrapTopA/B, on the treble case top at y 0.54) in a loose arc out to z -0.19 and back down to its bottom hook (shoulderStrapBottomA/B at y 0.04 on the back). The lowest point stays at y>=0.015. Each has a chrome slide buckle (a rectangular frame with a bar) at mid-height and a leather end tab with 3 small chrome rivets. Hooks are chrome U-shapes seated on the base plates the treble case builds. Build the arcs as a sweep over a catmull path or as a few segmented boxes. (b) The bass hand-strap: a leather pad (box 0.07 wide x 0.20 tall x 0.02 thick, in leather) centred at bassStrapPad on the back of the bass case, with a strapBlack strap across it, a chrome buckle, gold stitching dots along both edges, and two chrome mounting rivets at each end. (c) The bellows strap: strapBlack, 0.03 wide, anchored on the bass case top at bellowsStrapAnchor on a chrome base plate. It runs along the bellows top (y~0.495, x 0.2 to -0.06) lying flat, ending in a leather tab at bellowsStrapKeeper with a chrome snap stud, and a chrome buckle at x~0.10. A small goldBright tassel (a cone with a 6-sided cap and 3 short rods) hangs from the buckle toward +Z off the bellows front edge. (d) a tiny labelCream tag on the left shoulder strap with a black dot pattern.
parts.attaches: Hooks sit on the treble back plates at shoulderStrapTopA/B and shoulderStrapBottomA/B. The hand strap pad sits on the bass back at bassStrapPad. The bellows strap starts at bellowsStrapAnchor on the bass top and ends at bellowsStrapKeeper on the bellows top.

calls.reasoning:
I'm designing a spec for a piano accordion in an Italian mother-of-pearl style, keeping it as a static object with no joints since it's just a prop. I'm working out realistic proportions, figuring roughly 0.40 m width, and thinking through how it would stand or be positioned on the floor.

Now I'm working out the model's orientation -- deciding whether the bellows axis runs along X with the bass end facing -X and the treble keyboard facing +X, and how the front grille and keyboard would face relative to the +Z direction to match a natural playing position.

I'm working out the keyboard orientation on the treble end face—trying to figure out which direction the keys protrude and how pitch ascends, since in actual playing position the fingers approach from one side with the long axis of the keys running toward the player.

I'm still trying to pin down the correct orientation of the keyboard bars—whether the keys' long axis runs front-to-back or toward the player's hand—based on how the keytops appear in real accordion photos, treating the rows as levers angled from a flat surface.

Working out dimensions: white key width times 24 gives roughly 0.5m height, matching real accordion treble cases around 0.45-0.5m tall. I'm settling on both treble and bass boxes at about 0.52m tall, with depth around 0.25-0.30m and a modest bellows length, plus adding straps for realism.

Now I'm placing the two boxes on the floor with the bellows connecting them at the bottom, keyboard on the vertical face, and the grille facing forward toward the audience—working out the x/y/z extents so the treble box sits correctly on the right side.

I'm working out the bass box extent with buttons included, landing on roughly 0.74 x 0.54 depth proportions, then adjusting the z-depth so the boxes and bellows folds with corner guards fit within a total size around [0.74, 0.54, 0.28].

Now I'm placing the shoulder straps and bass strap flush against the back near z -0.145 to -0.16, keeping boxes resting at z -0.15..0.15. For the finish, I'm going with Italian pearl styling: iridescent mother-of-pearl celluloid in cream, pale pink, aqua, and lilac tones with chrome or gold trim and red/black bellows accented by white pearl corners, building the celluloid as a mosaic of subtly varied pearl-color patches.

I'm adding gold filigree details — a fan-slotted grille, rosette, register switches on the treble top, a fictional "Bellini" logo plate, rhinestones, brass corner guards, gold-leaf bellows edges, and a buckled bass-end bellows strap with an air button, plus a 120-button bass side arranged in six rows of round pearl-topped buttons on the +X face.

Now I'm breaking the accordion into separate parts: the treble box with its pearl-shell body, keyboard, top register switches, and front gold fan grille, and the bass box with its own pearl detailing.

Next is the bass button plate, front grille, straps, and air valve button, followed by the red folded bellows with pleated edges, corner guards, strap, and latch. I'm also figuring out how to handle the straps and hardware—shoulder straps, hand strap, bellows strap—since they span multiple boxes, planning to group them into one harness part positioned along the back plane to avoid overlap conflicts.

I'm reconsidering the breakdown: rather than lumping everything into four parts, I could split the treble side into a case (body, grille, top registers, mosaic) and a separate keyboard part (keys and panel projecting outward), giving five parts total—trebleCase, keyboard, bellows, bassCase, and harness—to better separate ownership of ornamental details like pearl mosaic, gold filigree, and rhinestones.

I'm settling on five parts with a rough polygon budget: trebleCase 200, keyboard 120, bellows 220, bassCase (with buttons and grille) 220, and harness (straps, thumb strap, bellows latch) 100, totaling around 860. I'm now working out floor-level coordinates for each case, deciding whether to add small chrome feet or rubber pads at the base so the cases rest properly at y=0.

Now I'm placing the bellows between the two cases, slightly raised off the floor with corner guards and gold edge trim, and starting to lay out the keyboard section projecting off the treble case's face with white and black keys.

I'm working out the orientation of the keyboard — figuring out which side the player sits on and therefore which end of the keys should have the raised black-key portion, so the geometry near the front versus back matches a real piano layout.

I'm working out the treble case layout: front face gets the gold fan-slotted grille, the top face carries the register switches, and pearl paneling wraps around the keyboard end, top, bottom, and back.

Now I'm settling on a limited color palette — soft pearl whites, creams, pinks, aquas and lilacs for the iridescent case, warm golds for the grille and trim, chrome tones for hardware, and deep reds for the bellows, plus black and key colors for contrast.

I'm also working out the positioning coordinates for key components like the bellows faces, keyboard plane, and bass button plane, figuring out where each piece sits relative to the case geometry.

Now I'm working out the harness strap placement — anchoring shoulder straps to the treble case back at top and bottom points, then draping them as an arc behind the case to approximate how straps hang loosely in a real display mount.

For the bass side, I'm adding a leather hand strap across the back with a buckle, then positioning the bellows strap on the bass case front-lower area with a chrome clasp and loose hanging tail, matching how the real accordion's bellows strap would sit when open.

I should fix the layout to be symmetric around x=0: treble case spanning -0.35 to -0.14 with keys to -0.38, bellows centered from -0.14 to 0.14, and bass from 0.14 to 0.35 with buttons extending to 0.38.

For the bellows itself, I'm planning 14 folds across a 0.28 length, each rendered as paired tapered slabs forming alternating ridges and valleys, with crests scaled outward and valleys inset slightly, colored in alternating red tones with gold accents on the ridges to match the Italian accordion aesthetic.

I'm also adding corner guards — gold or chrome plates with rivet details at the bellows corners — plus pearl-colored end frames where the bellows meets each case, keeping everything static since the instrument doesn't need articulated joints.

For the pearl mosaic pattern, I'm standardizing a tile system across both case boxes: small raised tiles around 0.035 in size, mostly pearl white with a mix of cream, pink, aqua, and lilac accents, separated by thin gaps revealing a shadow underlay, plus rhinestone corners and gold piping along the edges for consistency. For the grille, I'm designing a bezel-framed panel with a recessed dark backing plate and gold bars radiating outward in a fan pattern.

Now I'm fleshing out the treble side's details -- adding a central rosette with a "BELLINI" logo plate, a row of register switches with chrome plate and gold-labeled rocker tabs on top, a decorative gold strip, and on the back a chrome plate with serial number and strap-hook mounts, while laying out coordinate positions for the bellows face mount points.

Adding strap anchor and bellows keeper positions, then working out the keyboard geometry: the box spans roughly y 0.03 to 0.51 giving 24 white keys at about 0.02 spacing, with black keys placed in the standard C#/D# gap, F#/G#/A# pattern between them, plus considering whether a pearl frame should outline the keyboard slot.

Now I'm laying out the keyboard assembly in more detail -- gold rails along the top and bottom edges, a felt key bed, 24 white keys and 17 black keys totaling 41, which checks out. I'm also sketching the bass side case dimensions and figuring the button layout, likely six rows for a standard 120-bass configuration.

Working out button positions and materials...

I'll make the C-note buttons chrome and marked distinctly, keeping the rest pearl white, and merge instances to stay within the part budget. I also need to add the bass air-valve button near the top corner of the button plate as a gold-ringed pearl-red accent, plus gold slats and a rosette on the bass front grille with gold trim along the top.

I'm planning the bellows pleats with gold-wire leaf details, then designing the harness: black shoulder straps with chrome buckles and gold stitching, leather end tabs and hooks, a stitched bass hand strap with chrome buckle, a bellows strap with a snap and small hanging gold tassel, and a "BELLINI" nameplate on the treble side. I'm tallying the part budget, which comes to around 900 total.

Now I'm working out the JSON structure, setting the floor flags for treble and bass true while others stay false, and computing bounding boxes for the harness straps and bellows strap anchors based on their positions along the instrument.

I'm planning a static keyboard build using merged boxes by color, positioning it on the case's -X face with keys extending outward, and working out the spacing for 24 white keys stacked along the Y axis with a 0.02 pitch.

For the black keys, I'm figuring out the F-sharp-starting pattern of sharps/flats across the 24 white keys, checking modular arithmetic on index positions to confirm it yields the correct count of 17 black keys grouped in the standard 3-2-3-2... alternating clusters with gaps for the natural half-steps.

Now I'm thinking through structuring the model as merged geometry boxes without any joint/bone hierarchy, since a static model doesn't require bones.

I'm deciding whether to merge keys by color into just a few parts, or keep them as individual pieces for more detail—given the part budget, merging per color is simpler. I'm also considering adding small design touches like a beveled front lip on the white keys for visual detail where the viewer sees the key ends.

I'm working through the black key geometry now, trying to figure out which axis represents the key's length versus thickness, and where the tip bevel wedge should sit given the ambiguous orientation relative to the player.

Still shaping the wedge geometry...

Shaping the tip wedge...

Now I need to handle merging geometries from different sources—ExtrudeGeometry and BoxGeometry have incompatible structures, so I'm writing a helper to convert everything to non-indexed, strip UV attributes, and combine them with mergeGeometries.

I'm also working out small highlight strip boxes for the black key tops, figuring out thin x-width strips positioned along the z-length to sit on the top face.

Then I'm placing a felt slab box behind the white keys spanning the full y and z range, accounting for the small gaps between keys given their height vs pitch spacing. I'm also setting up the top and bottom rails in gold, deciding their x and y extents relative to the key frame.

Adding the groove line and pearl-mosaic cap rail geometry...

I'll go with the mosaic rule's colour distribution (mostly pearlWhite/cream with small accent percentages) rather than a single pearlCream tile, merging tiles by colour group to keep part count low—roughly 30 tiles per face type across both rails, grouped into about 5 colour parts, each tile a simple 12-triangle box.

Now for the gold piping, I'm thinking through where a thin gold rod can run without eating into the tile space—placing it along the outer corner edge of the rail rather than the inner face so the mosaic still fits within the available width.

Working out the exact placement of the piping rod and tiles on the -X face, trying tight margins around the 0.1155-0.125 z range while keeping everything inside the rail bounds. I decide the rails can be slightly wider since the box limit is ±0.125, and the felt slab spans ±0.115 with cap rails sitting right at the edge from 0.115 to 0.125.

Now I'm sketching the top/bottom rail geometry in gold, spanning z ±0.125 with cap rails running the full y-length, then placing corner rhinestone gems near the four frame corners on the -X rail face to accent the edges.

I'll add tiny rhinestones at the four corners plus small gold dot trim, keeping the rail detailing simple with just a goldDeep groove and gem rather than full rivet rows. I'm also placing a labelCream felt strip with a goldDeep line in the gap between the key ends and the +Z rail, positioned along the case's y-axis span.

I'm checking that the black keys stop at z=0.10 so they don't overlap the key-cover strip starting at 0.1025, which works out fine. I'll skip adding a back felt strip since it's not essential for symmetry, and now I'm thinking about small pitch-marker dots on the C white keys—placing a tiny goldBright cylinder near the exposed end of each white key as a marker.

Adding a bottom shading strip too, though I realize it'll mostly get hidden behind the black keys where they overlap at the boundary—acceptable since it's a minor visual detail.

Thinking about whether to add a thin goldDeep shadow rod filling the gap between the top rail and the topmost key, around y 0.5085–0.51, to make the transition look more grounded; need to check if the same treatment applies at the bottom rail near y 0.03.

Now I'm setting up the mosaic tile system: a seeded RNG picks colors per tile from a palette, with tiles grouped by color into geometry lists, starting with the base slab boxes for the cap rails on each side.

For the y-direction, 15 tiles at 0.032 pitch fit the 0.48 span with 0.03 tile height and 0.002 gaps. For the outer side faces, I'm reworking the z-range so tiles sit just inside the box limit instead of exceeding it — shrinking the base to 0.115-0.123 and placing tiles from 0.123-0.125, then mirroring this approach for the -X face with adjusted x-bounds.

Still working out tile coordinates...

Working out the rail geometry along y 0.03..0.51 with gold top/bottom bands, deciding to keep the piping rod confined to that same y range so it sits cleanly within the rail rather than extending over it. Then placing corner rhinestones near the top rail's -X face, positioned just adjacent to the piping at roughly y=0.515.

Placing the gems using small faceted octahedron-like geometry with alternating colors by z position, mirroring the same setup for the bottom rail at y=0.025. I'm also considering adding a thin goldDeep shadow strip along the rail's -X face as an inlay detail, running the length of the rail at both top and bottom.

Tallying up the parts now — felt, white/black keys, bevel strips, rails, gold inlays, gems, piping, dots — roughly 22 pieces, which feels like a reasonable balance between richness and complexity. I could go further with individual per-key highlights and gloss lines for extra polish since quality is the priority here.

Thinking about small refinements: a thin gold line along the back felt margin, symmetric on both sides, plus tiny gold screw heads on the rails near the ends and center, merged with the deep gold material for consistency.

Writing box helper code...

I need a merge function that normalizes geometries before combining them—converting to non-indexed and stripping UVs so attributes match across box, extrude, cylinder, and icosahedron shapes. I should guard against calling toNonIndexed on already non-indexed geometry since that triggers a warning in newer Three.js versions.

For the black key wedges, I'm defining a tapered shape in local coordinates with absolute x positions and y offsets centered on each key, then extruding it along z with a small depth and positioning it slightly above the white keys.

Now I'm adding a thin darker strip along the top of each black key to catch the light, positioning it to match the wedge's taper near the tip.

I'll settle on a thin highlight strip running along z at x center -0.378, width 0.006, spanning z from 0 to 0.095, and skip adding a second bevel strip. Now I'm working out the y-positions for each white key, placing them with a small gap so the lowest key sits flush against the rail and the top key ends at 0.5085, then moving to figure out the black key placement.

I'm computing the black key centers to align with the gaps between white keys, centering each at roughly 0.04925+0.02i, then moving on to write the tile coloring logic that randomly assigns white, cream, pink, aqua, or lilac tiles, and setting up the loop to place tiles symmetrically on both sides.

Still placing coordinates...

Then I'm adding small pitch dot cylinders along the key edge and bevel highlight/shadow strips on the white key end faces, picking slightly different shades to simulate light catching the beveled edge.

Now I'm setting up the gold fill box near the key gap and starting to write the actual geometry-building code, using a bucket map keyed by color to merge geometries efficiently before export.

I'm planning the buildBellows function using the provided Ctx type, designing an accordion-like bellows structure running along the X axis with 13 pleats spanning from -0.14 to 0.14.

I'm working out the cross-section dimensions and placing crests and valleys so the ends terminate cleanly against end frames, then calculating how many slabs and corner rods this would require against a 200-part budget. Since that's too many parts, I'm rethinking the approach to merge geometries by color into single static pieces without joints, keeping everything on one unparented part.

Writing slab geometry code...

I'm refining the facet coloring further: splitting each valley-to-crest facet into two segments, with the lower portion colored light or dark depending on orientation, and a narrower band near the crest colored solid red to make the ridge read clearly. Then I'm working out how these colored rectangle segments assemble into rings around all four sides, joining properly at the corners.

Now I'm computing the geometry for the inset quads connecting adjacent rings, making sure shared corner points keep the surface continuous, and figuring out a small inward extrusion thickness toward the central axis to give the pleats a bit of depth.

I'm adjusting the frame inner opening dimensions so the valley ring stays visible with a felt gasket gap, then adding a thin black cap/gasket piece behind the opening to show dark interior depth at the bellows end.

Now I'm planning the frame as four pearlCream boxes (top, bottom, front, back) with gold piping rods placed along both the inner and outer edges.

For merging geometries across different colors, I need a helper that normalizes all shapes by stripping UV attributes and converting to non-indexed form before combining them with BufferGeometryUtils, tracking rotated boxes with their transform matrices applied. I'll organize everything into a color-keyed accumulator map that collects geometries before the final merge.

Still arranging the crest rods...

I should also place a lozenge marker on the center pleat crest, which lands exactly at x=0 since it's pleat index 6 of 13. Since the crest is a ridge rather than a flat face, I need to work out how to position the diamond shape across the sloped facets so it sits properly on the V-shaped ridge.

Placing smaller diamonds above and below, then adding a darker gold outline layer behind for depth, plus small rose rhinestone gems flanking the crests of neighboring pleats, with thin wire tracing the crest line between them.

Placing guards on the 7 crest positions along x, centered on each corner crest, I'm designing an L-shaped bracket from two small boxes: one thin box covering the top face near the corner, and another covering the front face, joined to wrap around the edge.

Working out the corner plates now—for each of the four corners I need a horizontal plate wrapping over the ridge in z and a vertical plate wrapping in y, sizing each to span just past the corner point so they overlap cleanly against the crest geometry.

Still placing gold rivet cylinders at each corner bracket, and thinking about whether to add a thin gold piping accent alternating on every other pearl L-bracket for visual contrast.

Now I'm adding black reinforcing tape strips along the top surface at each valley fold, positioning thin black boxes that sit slightly proud of the groove to simulate taped seams across the interior valleys.

I'm checking whether the gold leaf dots placed in the front valleys would actually stay visible or get swallowed by the surrounding facet walls—since the groove geometry rises steeply from the valley, a dot of that radius risks being hidden unless it sits proud enough above the crease.

So I'll place each dot as a small low-poly sphere centered just above the valley floor, sized to fit the groove's width at that height, and repeat this for each valley to get a scattering of gold beads along the front.
